text: It is 1945, in Kaira district, Gujarat. Your village farmers keep buffaloes, and most families have only one or two litres of milk to sell each day. The government of Bombay has started the Bombay Milk Scheme. Milk travels 427 km from Anand to Bombay. A private dairy, Polson, holds the contract. But no one has fixed the price paid to farmers. The milk contractors pay whatever they like.

The government makes money from the scheme. Polson keeps a good margin. The contractors take the biggest cut. Farmers get what is left. Milk spoils fast, so they must sell at whatever price they are offered. The freedom leader Sardar Patel has given your farmers advice: build your own co-operative, with your own plant. If the government says no, stop selling milk, even if it hurts for a while.
How do you fight for a fair price?
Milk spoils in hours. Whoever owns the plant decides the price.
Our estimate: the talks drag on. Farmers keep getting low prices and some lose hope. Your union does start, but later and smaller than it could have been.

Talking without pressure gave the buyers no reason to change. The farmers stayed weak while you waited. What would have worked: Organise every village and be ready to stop supplying. The milk was the only real power the farmers had.

On 4 January 1946, at a meeting in Samarkha village, farmers agreed: every village would form a milk society, and all of them would join one Union that owned its own plant. The government said no. So the farmers went on a milk strike for 15 days. Not a drop of milk was sold to the traders. No milk reached Bombay from Anand, and the Bombay Milk Scheme almost collapsed. The government gave in. Your Union was registered on 14 December 1946.
Alone, each farmer had no power. Together, and owning the plant, they controlled the milk Bombay needed.
Our estimate: the government promises to look into it. The contractors still decide what farmers get, and a fair price never comes. Farmers start to say that nothing will ever change.

You asked others to fix your problem and kept the same middlemen. Nothing in the system changed. What would have worked: Unite the farmers in their own co-operative, own the plant, and be ready to stop selling.

It is June 1948. Your Union starts to pasteurise milk for Bombay. At first it is just two village societies and about 250 litres a day. Any farmer can join, whatever their caste or religion. A sure market is a big pull. By the end of the year 432 farmers have joined, and you handle 5,000 litres a day.
Our estimate: it is 1948. Your union is finally running, but only in a few villages. Farmers who saw the contractors win are slow to trust you, and growth is slow.

It is 1953. In winter, buffaloes give about two and a half times more milk than in summer. Bombay cannot take all of it. Your farmers are selling the extra milk cheap to middlemen again. And experts around the world say buffalo milk has too much fat to turn into milk powder.
What do you do with the extra winter milk?
The buffalo does not take a holiday. Your farmers cannot either.
Our estimate: farmers pour away milk or sell it cheap to traders. Many stop trusting the union, because it is not there when they need it most.

A co-operative that turns away its members' milk breaks its main promise: a sure market, every day. What would have worked: Find a way to use every litre: make products that keep, like butter and milk powder.
Our estimate: the milk gets used, but the private buyers set a low winter price. Farmers earn something, and the middlemen are back in the game.

It solved this winter, but it handed the price back to the people you had just escaped. What would have worked: Build your own factory to turn the extra milk into butter and powder, so the value stays with the farmers.

The government of India helped the Union get money from UNICEF and help from New Zealand, with technical aid from the FAO. A Rs 50 lakh factory for milk powder and butter was planned. The President of India laid its foundation stone on 15 November 1954. In 1955 a dairy engineer at Anand installed a spray-dryer for buffalo milk, which Amul describes as the first in the world. Experts had said buffalo milk could not be dried. In 1955 the Prime Minister opened the factory. Now the Union could take farmers' milk all year round.
You turned the problem into a product. Milk that went bad in hours became butter and powder that could keep and travel.

Your new dairy makes butter and milk powder from buffalo milk, which Amul says was a first in the world. You sell them under one name: Amul, from the Sanskrit word 'Amulya', which means priceless. In the years that follow, Amul also makes cheese and baby food from buffalo milk.

Our estimate: after more hard winters, you build a smaller butter plant, years late. You sell under one name, Amul, from the Sanskrit word for priceless. But private dairies already have a head start.

It is October 1964. The Prime Minister comes to Anand to open your new cattle feed plant. He spends a night in a village with your farmers. He sees how well it works, and he wants your model copied across India.
Our estimate: it is 1964. Your union is smaller than it could be, but it works. The Prime Minister visits Anand, and he wants farmers across India to have something like it.
What do you do with what you have learned?
One district cannot feed a country. But a good model can travel.

In 1965 the National Dairy Development Board was set up at Anand to copy the Amul model across India. It later drew up Operation Flood, the biggest dairy program in the world. It was built on what people called the 'Anand Pattern': a society in each village, a union in each district, and a federation in each state.
You gave away the recipe, not the business. Farmers everywhere got their own co-operatives, and the whole movement grew stronger.
Our estimate: Kaira's farmers do well, but the rest of India stays in the hands of middlemen. Without a national movement, big private dairies grow strong enough to squeeze even you.

Farmers in other states were not your rivals. The middlemen were. Keeping the model to yourself left you alone. What would have worked: Help other farmers build co-operatives of their own, so that farmers, not traders, run India's milk.
Our estimate: Amul grows big, but farmers far away are just suppliers to a dairy in Gujarat. They do not own it, so they do not feel it is theirs.

Growth helped, but farmers who do not own the dairy have no reason to stay loyal when a trader offers more. What would have worked: Let farmers in every state own their own co-operatives on the same model, and link them together.
It is 1966. Amul Butter's ads use an old line: 'Purely the Best'. You want families in every city to ask for Amul by name.
How do you sell your butter to India's homes?
People forget a product. They remember a friend.
Our estimate: the ads are correct and safe. People see them, but they do not talk about them, and the butter still looks like any other brand.
Plain facts tell people what you sell. They do not make people care. What would have worked: Give the brand a face and a voice, something people look forward to seeing.
Our estimate: you save money, but big private brands fill the cities with their ads. Shoppers pick the name they know, and it is not yours.
A good product nobody has heard of loses to an average product everyone knows. What would have worked: Spend on a smart, cheap campaign that makes your brand a friend of the family.

In 1966 Amul hired the head of an ad agency to make a new campaign for Amul Butter. He created a little girl mascot to win over mothers and children. Her first topical ad made a joke about horse racing. From 1967 she began to joke about the news of the day, on big roadside boards. The campaign later set a Guinness World Record as the longest-running ad campaign in the world.
A funny, friendly mascot made a farmers' product feel like part of the family, and the news gave her something new to say every week.

On 13 January 1970 Operation Flood begins. Its first phase is paid for with milk powder and butter oil given by Europe through the World Food Programme. It links 18 milk areas to Delhi, Bombay, Calcutta and Madras. In Gujarat, other districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha have built milk unions just like yours.
Our estimate: it is 1970. In most of India, milk is still run by middlemen. But in Gujarat, other districts like Mehsana and Banaskantha have built milk unions of their own.
Our estimate: it is 1973. Even without your help, Gujarat's other milk unions have grown. Now they fight with you and with each other in the same towns, each one paying for its own ads.
It is 1973. Gujarat's milk unions all grew from the same idea. But now they compete with each other in the same markets, each one paying for its own ads.
How should Gujarat's milk unions sell?
Farmers fighting farmers is a gift to every big company.
Our estimate: you cut prices to beat the other unions. Farmers in every district earn less, and private dairies smile as the co-operatives weaken each other.

Your real competitors were the big private dairies. A war between farmers only made all farmers poorer. What would have worked: Join forces: one federation, one brand, one budget, with every union owning a share.

In 1973 the unions set up the Gujarat Co-operative Milk Marketing Federation, GCMMF, to sell for all of them. They pooled their strength, cut ad costs and stopped competing with each other. The Kaira Union handed its Amul brand over to the federation. Now farmers owned their village societies, the societies owned the district unions, and the unions owned the federation.
One brand gave millions of small farmers the power of one big company, while they still owned every part of it.
Our estimate: you save some money on trucks, but shoppers see five or six milk names from Gujarat. Each one is too small to stand up to the big brands.
Sharing costs helped, but the brands still split the shopper's attention and the ad money. What would have worked: Put everything under one brand, so every rupee spent on ads helps every farmer.

In 1976 GCMMF made a film about the milk co-operatives, Manthan. It was paid for by 500,000 farmers, who gave two rupees each. By the end of 1985, 4.25 million milk producers were part of 43,000 village co-operatives. In 1998 India became the largest milk producer in the world. Today 3.6 million milk producers control GCMMF, and Amul is still their brand.
Our estimate: you took a slightly different road, but you kept the farmers united and in charge. Their co-operative grows into one of India's best-known food brands.
Our estimate: the farmers keep their union and earn more than in the days of the contractors. But without one strong brand and a national plan, private dairies keep most of India's big city markets.
Our estimate: the farmers stay divided, and the middlemen and big dairies win again. Your union shrinks to a small local dairy, and most farmers still sell milk at whatever price they are offered.
Our estimate: after three costly calls, the union's elected board loses its trust in you and chooses someone else to lead the farmers.

It is late 1996. You run Apple, the maker of the Mac computer. In the year to September 1996, Apple lost $816 million. For years it has promised new software to run the Mac, and that software is still not ready.

The Mac needs a modern operating system, the main software that runs a computer. Your own project, called Copland, has been shelved after years of delays. Be, a young company, has fast new software, but it is still being tested. NeXT, the company Apple's co-founder started in 1985, has mature software that is good at networks and at running many programs at once.
Where do you get the Mac's new software?
You can't sell tomorrow's computers on yesterday's software. And you can't wait much longer.
Our estimate: the team works hard, but the software keeps slipping. Buyers are tired of promises, and rivals keep moving while you wait.

Apple had already broken many promises about Copland. Giving a late project more time rarely makes it early. What would have worked: Buy software that already works, and spend your time making it a great Mac.
On 20 December 1996, Apple agreed to buy NeXT for $400 million. Apple said NeXT's software was the clear choice for the next Mac system. Apple's co-founder came back as an adviser to the CEO.
You bought software that was already mature, and you got back a founder who knew Apple and had built a company since.
Our estimate: you get clever new software and a small, bright team. But it needs years of work before ordinary buyers can use it, and the price is high for a young company.

Be's software was promising, but not finished. You paid a big price for more waiting. What would have worked: Buy software that is already proven, so your team can spend its time on the Mac, not on finishing someone else's work.

It is July 1997. Apple is still losing money. The CEO who bought NeXT resigns after 18 months. The money chief runs things day to day, and the returning co-founder gets a bigger role advising the board. Now you are the one making the calls.
Our estimate: it is mid-1997. Your new software is still far from ready, and the losses keep coming. The board replaces the CEO, and now you are the one making the calls.

It is August 1997, and Apple is losing money. For years Apple and Microsoft have fought in court over how the Mac looks. But Microsoft has also made software for the Mac since its early days, including its Office programs. Now Microsoft is ready to make peace and invest in Apple.
What do you do about Microsoft?
Your fans see Microsoft as the enemy. Your bank account may see it differently.
Our estimate: fans cheer, but lawyers cost money, and businesses worry that their work software may not run on Macs next year. Some of them stop buying.

You fought an old war while your company was running out of money. Pride does not pay salaries. What would have worked: Make peace, take the money and the promise of software, and spend your energy on great products.
Our estimate: you raise some cash, but at a high price, because lenders and investors know you are losing money. The court fight goes on, and buyers still wonder about Mac software.
Cash helps, but it does not end the fight or calm buyers who need their work software. What would have worked: Take the deal that brings cash, peace and software together.

On 6 August 1997 at Macworld Boston, Apple and Microsoft made a deal. Microsoft bought $150 million of Apple shares with no votes. The two shared their patents, Microsoft promised new Office versions for the Mac, and its web browser would become the Mac's default. Many fans in the hall booed. But Apple's share price rose 35% that day.
You put the company's survival above old pride. You got cash, peace and the software your buyers needed.

In September 1997 the board makes the returning co-founder interim CEO. You look at the product list. Apple sells dozens of Mac desktops, laptops and servers, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer. Few of them make money. Other companies also sell copies of the Mac, called clones, and pay Apple only $80 for each one.

You look at the product list. Apple sells dozens of Mac desktops, laptops and servers, plus printers, cameras and a hand-held computer. Few of them make money. Other companies also sell copies of the Mac, called clones, and pay Apple only $80 for each one.
What do you do with all these products?
Even shop staff can't explain which Mac to buy. If they can't, how can a customer?

Apple cut more than 70% of its products down to a simple grid of four boxes. It stopped letting others copy the Mac, and paid $10 million in cash and $100 million in shares for the main Mac business of Power Computing, a clone maker. Over 3,000 jobs went. In February 1998 it also stopped its hand-held Newton.
Focus is saying no. Four great products are easier to build, sell and explain than dozens of weak ones.
Our estimate: more Macs are sold, but more of them are cheap clones that earn you $80 each. Your own teams are spread thin, and your warehouses fill with products few people want.

You chased size instead of profit. Clones sold to your own customers, and too many products split your best people. What would have worked: Cut to a few products you can make great, and stop others selling cheaper copies of your best idea.
Our estimate: costs fall a little, but the product list is still confusing, and clone makers keep selling against you at lower prices.
A small trim feels safe, but it does not fix the real problem: too many products and copies of your own. What would have worked: Make a deep cut to a few clear products, and end the clone deals.
Sales of Mac computers have fallen by almost 20% in two years, and Apple is losing money. Money is tight, but the ad agency that made Apple's famous 1984 ad is ready to work with you again.
How do you talk to buyers now?
People don't just buy a computer. They buy what it says about them.
Our estimate: you save money this year, but silence looks like surrender. Shops give your computers less space, and buyers decide Apple really is finished.
When people think you are dying, silence proves them right. What would have worked: Spend on a clear message about who you are, even when money is tight.

On 28 September 1997, Apple's new "Think different" ads appeared on US TV, in the first network showing of the film Toy Story. They were made by the same agency as the 1984 ad. Apple said it was the start of a bigger push to show it was going back to its core values.
You reminded people why they loved Apple before you asked them to buy again.
Our estimate: some buyers notice the numbers, but rivals answer with their own numbers next month. Apple sounds like just another computer seller.
Fighting on specs plays the rival's game, where there are many more players and lower prices. What would have worked: Remind people what makes Apple different, then back it up with great products.

In October 1997, Apple reported a loss of $1 billion for the year. Sales fell 28%, to $7.1 billion. Much of the loss was one-time costs for reorganising and for buying NeXT and the clone business. Then, in the three months to December 1997, Apple made a profit of $47 million.
Our estimate: it is early 1998. Apple is still fighting to stop the losses, and the board wants proof that ordinary buyers will come back.
Your four-box plan has an empty box: a desktop for homes and schools. Apple needs something that brings in new buyers, not just old fans.
Apple needs a desktop for homes and schools, something that brings in new buyers, not just old fans.
What kind of home computer do you build?
Don't build what the market already has. Build what it doesn't know it wants yet.
Our estimate: your loyal buyers stay, but there are not enough of them. Each year the Mac becomes a smaller club, and app makers pay less attention to it.
A company that only sells to its fans slowly shrinks. You need new buyers to grow. What would have worked: Build a simple, striking computer that brings first-time buyers to the Mac.
Our estimate: it sells a little, but it gets lost on shop shelves full of beige boxes, and cheap PCs still win on price.
Copying the rival's look means fighting only on price, where you are weakest. What would have worked: Make a computer that looks and feels different, and is easy to get online with.

Apple showed the iMac on 6 May 1998, at $1,299. It had a see-through case, was built for the internet and dropped the floppy disk drive. It reached shops on 15 August 1998, and many stores sold out. In six weeks Apple sold 278,000, the fastest-selling Mac ever. Almost 3 in 10 early buyers had never owned a computer before.
You built something new, simple and easy to love, and it brought people to the Mac who had never owned a computer.

In the year to September 1998, Apple made a profit of $309 million, its first profitable year since 1995. Its cash grew to $2.3 billion. In the three months to December 1998 it sold 519,000 iMacs and made a profit. It was Apple's fifth profitable quarter in a row.
Our estimate: you fixed the software, focused the products and gave buyers a reason to believe. Apple is back to making money and has a clear future.
Our estimate: Apple survives, but it stays small and stuck. It makes a little money, yet buyers and app makers see it as a side choice, not the future.
Our estimate: the losses never stop and the cash runs out. Apple is sold off in pieces, and the Mac becomes a memory.
Our estimate: three costly calls in a row. The board has lost its trust in you and asks someone else to save Apple.
It is 2000. You run Blockbuster, with thousands of video shops across America. A small startup called Netflix rents DVDs by post. It is losing money, and its founders have come to see you.
Netflix wants Blockbuster to buy it for $50 million. Your stores bring in billions in revenue. Netflix has never made a profit.
What do you say?
Ask yourself what customers might want in five years, not what they want today.
Our estimate: your own online service starts small and slow, because store managers see it as a threat. But you learn about online rental years earlier than you otherwise would.

You saw the shift and started learning, which was smart. But building from zero is slower than buying a team that already knows how. What would have worked: Buy the startup for a small price, keep its team, and let it run separately from the stores.
Our estimate: for a small sum, for a company your size,, you own the most promising rental startup in America. Its team keeps building, away from the stores, and you now have a foot in the future.
$50 million was small for a company your size. Buying a fast-learning team is cheap insurance against your own business being disrupted.

Blockbuster said no. Netflix was losing money at the time, and according to one of its founders, Blockbuster saw it as a small niche business. Blockbuster did not launch its own online rental service in the US until August 2004.

Judging a startup only by its size today hides the real question: is it learning something your customers will want? What would have worked: Buy it cheaply and let it run on its own, or at least start your own online rental service right away.
Our estimate: it is 2004, your Netflix team is growing fast, and more people rent DVDs online every month. Your stores still bring in most of the money, but sales in them are starting to slip.
It is 2004. Blockbuster has over 9,000 stores and $6.1 billion in revenue. But in the first half of the year, sales in your existing stores fell 5.1%, and renting DVDs online is growing fast.
Your Netflix team wants more money to grow. Your store managers say online rental is stealing their customers.
Your small online service has a few loyal members. Now the market is big enough to matter.
Online rental is no longer a niche. You have no online service of your own.
What do you do about online rental?
Your stores are a strength no website has. The question is how to use them.
Our estimate: the shops look great, but each year fewer people drive to them. Online services keep growing without you.
Making the old business nicer does not stop customers moving to a new habit. What would have worked: Go online now and use your stores as something online-only rivals cannot match.

In August 2004 Blockbuster launched Blockbuster Online at $19.99 a month for three DVDs at a time, about $2 less than Netflix, with no late fees. It passed 1 million subscribers in under a year, but it was expensive: analysts expected it to add about $170 million to spending in 2005.

It was the right move, but it came four years after you turned Netflix down, and it was mostly a copy of Netflix. Being cheaper is a weak edge against a rival who got there first. What would have worked: Launch online and link it to your stores from day one, so you offer something no online-only rival can.
Our estimate: members get DVDs by post and can also return them at any store for a new movie on the spot. No online-only rival can offer that, and members flock to you.
You turned your biggest cost, thousands of stores, into a feature a website alone could not copy.

Our estimate: it is 2006, and members love swapping mailed DVDs in your stores. Blockbuster also ended late fees in January 2005, and in the first three months late-fee money fell by $128.5 million. Online is growing, but so are the costs.

It is 2006. Blockbuster ended late fees in January 2005. In the first three months, late-fee money fell by $128.5 million, and the company lost $57.5 million. In mid-2005 Netflix had about 3 million online members, against about 1 million for you.
Netflix is ahead online. You still have thousands of stores that Netflix does not.
How do you fight back?
Netflix cannot open a store tomorrow. You can let people walk into one tonight.
Our estimate: profits look better this year, but online members drift to Netflix and do not come back.

Saving cash by shrinking the part of the business that is growing only makes the shrinking part more important. What would have worked: Spend to link your stores and online service, the one thing your rival cannot copy.
Our estimate: more advertising brings some new members, but there is still no clear reason to choose you over Netflix.
Marketing a copy harder does not make it different. What would have worked: Give members something only you can offer: swap mailed DVDs in your stores.

On November 1, 2006, Blockbuster launched Total Access. Members could swap DVDs that came by post for free rentals in its stores, with plans from $5.99 a month. Subscribers grew strongly, but launch costs were higher than expected.
You finally used what Netflix did not have, your stores, to make the online service better. That is a real reason for customers to choose you.

It is 2007. Blockbuster's chief executive has left after a fight with the board over pay, and a new one takes over. Now you see the company through new eyes. From 2002 to 2005 Blockbuster lost over $4 billion. The free in-store swaps are popular, but they cost a lot of money.
Total Access is winning members from Netflix, but free in-store swaps are expensive. Investors want losses to stop.
Online is still behind Netflix, and investors want losses to stop.
What is your plan?
Cutting costs is easy. Cutting the right costs is the job.

The new CEO charged members $7 more a month for in-store swaps, and planned tests of new store layouts and of selling small electronics. Blockbuster lost 500,000 online subscribers in summer 2007, and its shares fell 17% after a November 2007 meeting with investors.

You raised the price on the one thing that made you different, just when customers were choosing between you and a rival. What would have worked: Keep the swaps cheap, close weak stores to save money, and invest the savings in movie downloads.
Our estimate: you shrink the store network carefully, keep members happy, and start building for a world where movies arrive over the internet, not on discs.
You cut the past to fund the future, and kept the feature customers loved.
Our estimate: costs fall fast, but every closed store means fewer places to swap DVDs, so online gets a little less special.
Cutting costs was needed, but you cut without a plan for what comes after discs. What would have worked: Close weak stores and put the savings into what comes next: movie downloads.
Our estimate: you moved early, used your stores as a weapon, and followed movies onto the internet. Blockbuster is still the name people think of for movie night.
Our estimate: you closed many stores, but your online service keeps a loyal group of members. Blockbuster survives as a smaller company.

In July 2010 the New York Stock Exchange stopped trading Blockbuster's shares. On September 23, 2010, Blockbuster filed for bankruptcy, with its 3,000 US stores still open. In April 2011 DISH Network bought its assets for about $320 million.
Three costly calls. The board has lost its trust in you and brings in someone else.

It is 2005. India opened its airline market to more competition in 2004, and about six new airlines have started. The economy is expected to grow about 6.9% this year, and air travel may grow up to 20% a year. You and a co-founder, backed by the travel group InterGlobe, plan a new low-cost airline. You have no planes and no flights yet.

Three airlines, Jet, Kingfisher and Air India, carry nearly 8 in 10 Indian flyers. Kingfisher is thinking big and has ordered giant superjumbo jets. Airbus says 100 million more Indians could become flyers by 2010. You are at the Paris Air Show, where airlines buy planes.
How do you build your fleet?
A small start feels safe. But in airlines, size and sameness can be the cheapest thing you buy.
Our estimate: you start flying with little risk. But used planes of different types need different spare parts and trained crews. Your costs stay close to your rivals', and growth is slow.

Starting small saves money today, but it gives you no cost edge over bigger airlines. What would have worked: Order many new planes of one type at once. A big order gets a better price, and one type keeps training and repairs simple.

On 16 June 2005, at the Paris Air Show, IndiGo ordered 100 Airbus A320 planes, worth $6 billion at list prices. It had not flown a single flight. The first plane arrived on 28 July 2006. On 4 August 2006, IndiGo flew its first flight, from Delhi to Imphal via Guwahati.
One big order of one plane type gave you a bulk price, simple training and simple repairs for years to come.
Our estimate: every plane type needs its own pilots, engineers and spare parts. Your costs climb before your first ticket is sold, and planes sit idle waiting for the right crew.

A mixed fleet adds cost everywhere: training, repairs, spare parts and scheduling. A low-cost airline cannot afford that. What would have worked: Pick one plane type and order it in bulk. Keep the fleet simple so every pilot and engineer can work on every plane.

It is 2006 and your first planes are arriving. Air Deccan, India's first low-cost airline, sells very cheap tickets but is struggling. Kingfisher is buying giant jets. And in India, a flight leaving 15 to 20 minutes late is normal.
What kind of airline will you be?
Ask what a normal Indian flyer really wants. Is it a free meal, or is it to reach the meeting on time?
Our estimate: flyers love the meals, but your costs are now as high as the big airlines'. You must charge their fares, and most flyers have no reason to pick a new name.

You copied the big airlines' costs without their size or fame. A new airline needs a clear reason to be chosen. What would have worked: Cut what flyers will not miss, like free meals and a business class, and give them what they care about most: low fares and on-time flights.
Our estimate: your planes fill up fast, but every seat sold below cost loses money. Rivals cut their fares too, and soon nobody is making money.

Low fares win flyers, but fares below cost only work while the cash lasts. A price war has no winner. What would have worked: Keep fares low by keeping costs low, not by losing money. Then win flyers with something rivals find hard to copy, like being on time.

IndiGo launched with one class only. No business seats, no free meals, no loyalty points. Snacks were for sale. Its big promise was simple: your flight leaves on time. Because every plane was an A320, pilots, crew and engineers worked faster, and a plane could be ready again in 20 to 30 minutes. In November 2009, 78.4% of IndiGo flights were on time, against 74.5% for all Indian airlines.
Our estimate: flyers like the low fares and the on-time promise. But with mixed or used planes, your ground teams work slower, and keeping the promise is harder than making it.
You cut what flyers would not miss and promised what they wanted most. A simple promise, kept every day, builds trust.
You have ordered 100 planes worth $6 billion at list prices. Six planes flew by the end of 2006, and nine more are joining in 2007. A young airline cannot pay for all of them from its own pocket.
Our estimate: your fleet is growing, and planes cost a lot of money. A young airline cannot pay for all of them from its own pocket.
How do you pay for your planes?
You need planes to fly, not planes to own. Think about what you really need.

IndiGo bought planes in bulk at a discount, sold them to leasing companies around the time they arrived, and leased them back. It gave planes back within about six years. This kept big loans off its books, brought cash in up front, and kept the fleet young, so fewer flights were delayed by repairs.
Our estimate: leasing companies pay you less, because you are not buying in bulk. Still, you free up cash and keep your planes fairly new.
You turned a huge bill into cash in hand, and young planes meant fewer repairs and fewer delays.
Our estimate: you own your planes, but you also own big loans. Every month the interest is due, even when flights fly half empty. And as your planes age, repair bills grow.

Owning planes ties up money and adds debt. In a business where profits swing, heavy debt is dangerous. What would have worked: Sell new planes to leasing companies and rent them back. You get cash up front and can swap old planes for new ones.
Our estimate: the rent is cheap, but old planes break down more often. They burn more fuel and spend more days in the repair shop. Your on-time record starts to slip.

Old planes look cheap but cost more in fuel, repairs and delays. For an airline that promises to be on time, that is a bad trade. What would have worked: Keep the fleet young. Sell new planes to leasing companies, rent them back, and swap them before they get old.

It is 2008. Fuel prices have shot up, and fares with them. In 2007 Kingfisher's parent company bought 26% of Air Deccan. Now Jet Airways and Kingfisher are working together to cut costs. This year, Indian airlines will lose $2.5 billion, a quarter of all airline losses in the world.
Some airlines sell tickets far below cost. India's tax on jet fuel is several times the world average. Rivals are joining hands to survive.
How do you get through the storm?
In a storm, everyone looks for a big move. Sometimes the big move is to keep doing the simple thing well.
Our estimate: you get more planes and routes overnight, but also their debts, their mixed fleet and their late flights. Your teams spend a year fixing someone else's problems.

Buying a weak rival in a downturn means buying its losses too. It breaks the simple model that made you strong. What would have worked: Stay on your own. Keep your simple model and tight costs, and let weaker rivals shrink.

IndiGo kept flying only A320s, with one class and tight costs, and kept adding planes. Its 25th plane arrived in 2009. In the year to March 2009, IndiGo made a profit of $17.6 million. In the same year Kingfisher lost $342.7 million, Jet Airways lost $86.1 million and SpiceJet lost $75.4 million.
Our estimate: staying calm helps, but your costs are higher than they could be. You lose a little money this year, though far less than the rivals who panicked.
When everyone else was chasing size, you protected the low costs that let you make money even in a bad year.
Our estimate: you save on fuel, but parked planes still cost rent. Flyers and travel agents get used to other airlines on your old routes.

Shrinking saves cash in the short run, but you give away routes and flyers that are hard to win back. What would have worked: If your costs are the lowest, keep flying. A low-cost airline can make money when others cannot, and take their flyers.
It is the end of 2010. IndiGo is now India's third-biggest airline, carrying 17.3% of flyers, ahead of Air India. Airbus has just launched a new version of the A320, called the A320neo.
Our estimate: it is the end of 2010. You have survived the bad years, but you are not yet among India's biggest airlines. Airbus has just launched a new version of the A320, called the A320neo.
Only a few Indians fly today, so the room to grow is huge. Newer planes need fewer repairs and burn less fuel. And in January 2011, you get a licence to fly abroad.
What do you order next?
The plan that got you here is simple. Do you scale it, change it, or rest?
Our estimate: your bank balance looks good, but in a few years you run out of planes to grow with. Rivals take the new routes first.

Saving cash is safe, but planes take years to arrive. A pause today means no growth in five years. What would have worked: Lock in a big order of the same plane type now, while you have the cash and the bargaining power.
Our estimate: big jets need new pilots, new engineers and new spare parts. Long flights fight strong foreign airlines. Your simple, low-cost model gets complicated overnight.

Adding a second, very different plane type breaks the one-type model that kept your costs low. What would have worked: Stay with one plane type. Grow at home and fly to nearby countries with the same planes.

On 12 January 2011, IndiGo agreed to buy 180 more planes: 150 A320neo and 30 A320, worth $15.6 billion at list prices. Airbus called it the largest single firm order for big jets in its history. IndiGo was one of the first buyers of the A320neo. On 1 September 2011, it flew its first international flight, from Delhi to Dubai.
Our estimate: a big order of one plane type gives you a good price and room to grow. But your earlier choices mean you start this new chapter with less money and a weaker name than you could have.
You scaled the model that worked, with the same plane type, at a bulk price, years before you needed the planes.

By October 2011, IndiGo carried 19.6% of Indian flyers and was the only big Indian airline making a profit. In October 2012 Kingfisher's planes stopped flying, and its licence was suspended, with debts estimated at about $2.49 billion. IndiGo added flights. In 2012 it carried more passengers than any other Indian airline, and in the year to March 2013 its profit rose six times, to Rs 7.87 billion.
Our estimate: you made enough smart calls to pull ahead. Your simple, on-time airline becomes one of India's biggest, while rivals with heavy costs struggle.
Our estimate: your airline survives the hard years, but it is one of many. With higher costs than it could have had, it never pulls clearly ahead of its rivals.
Our estimate: high costs and debts catch up with you. Like several Indian airlines of this time, your planes go back to their owners and your flights stop.
Our estimate: three costly calls in a row. The board loses its trust in you and asks someone else to fly the airline through the storm.

It is 1982. In 1970 Intel made the 1103, one of the first DRAM memory chips sold to the public. It was the first chip to seriously challenge the old magnetic memory in computers. Memory chips built your company. Last year IBM launched its first PC, and inside it is your 8088 processor. But in Japan, makers like NEC, Hitachi and Fujitsu now get up to 40% more good chips from each batch than US makers do, at lower cost.

The IBM PC is selling far better than anyone expected. IBM's buyers made you find a second company, AMD, to also make your processors, so they never run short. Now IBM offers to buy 12% of Intel for $250 million.
What do you do with IBM's offer?
Money is useful. What you spend it on matters more.
Our estimate: you build more memory lines and cut your prices. Japanese makers, with better yields, cut even deeper. The $250 million melts away in a price war you cannot win.

You put fresh money into the business where you were already losing on cost. Money cannot fix a cost gap that big. What would have worked: Put the money where you are ahead: research and factories for processors, the chips inside the PC.

In December 1982 IBM agreed to pay $250 million, or $40 a share, for 12% of Intel. Intel said the money would go to research and more production capacity. The two companies were now tied closely together. In 1983 IBM also won the right to make some Intel chips itself.
You took cash from your most important customer and put it into the future: research and capacity for the PC boom.
Our estimate: you keep full freedom, but you have less cash for new factories just as demand starts to boom. Borrowing costs you more, and you build less than you could.

Independence has value, but turning away cheap money from your best customer slowed your growth when it mattered. What would have worked: Take the investment, keep control of your decisions, and spend the money on research and capacity.

Our estimate: IBM's money went into memory lines, and you are still behind Japan on cost. Now the PC boom of 1983 and 1984 is ending. Orders collapse, and there are far too many chips. For five years DRAM memory has been a small part of what you sell. Processors are now your core.

The PC boom of 1983 and 1984 is ending fast. At the end of 1984 orders collapse, and there are far too many chips in the world. Japanese makers still make memory chips better and cheaper. For five years DRAM memory has been a small part of what you sell. Processors are now your core.
What do you do about memory chips?
Be honest. Are you staying because it pays, or because it is your history?
Our estimate: the new factory takes two years and a lot of cash to build. By the time it runs, prices have fallen again, and Japanese rivals have moved to the next, bigger chip.

You bet a fortune on catching up in a race your rivals were already winning, during a price crash. What would have worked: Stop pouring money into memory and move your best factories to processors, where you lead.

Intel stayed in the memory chip business through 1984 and into 1985. Prices did not recover. They kept falling in 1985. A 256K memory chip sold for less than $3, and Intel expected heavy losses to go on.

Waiting felt safe, but it only made the losses last longer. Prices were falling for deep reasons, not bad luck. What would have worked: Accept that memory is lost, leave early, and give the factories to processors.
Our estimate: it hurts to walk away from the product that built Intel. But you stop the losses a year early and put your best factories to work on processors.
You looked at the numbers, not your history. Leaving early saved money and time for the business with a future.
Our estimate: your new memory factory is running, but prices fall faster than your costs. Japan makes most of the world's memory chips. Every chip you sell loses money.

In 1970 Intel made one of the first DRAM memory chips sold to the public. Now Japan makes most of the world's memory chips, and a 256K chip sells for under $3. DRAM memory is less than 5% of your business.
What do you do with your memory chips?
The business that made you is not always the business that will keep you.
Our estimate: trade talks take years. Meanwhile you keep losing money on every memory chip, and your best factory space stays tied up making them.

Help from the government might slow rivals down, but it does not fix your own costs. You stayed in a race you had already lost. What would have worked: Leave DRAM, keep only the products where you lead, and give your factories to processors.

In 1985 Intel left the DRAM business. It said too many factories around the world had pushed prices to levels it could not accept. Intel kept EPROMs, a chip it had invented, and won more of that market in 1985 and 1986. It also complained that Japanese makers sold EPROMs below cost, and a US trade body agreed.
You let go of the product that built Intel, but kept the part that still made money and freed your factories for processors.
Our estimate: you get out of memory cleanly, but you also give up EPROMs, a chip you invented and still lead in. You lose a steady stream of money just when you need it most.
Leaving the losing part was right. Leaving the winning part too threw away cash for no reason. What would have worked: Cut only what is losing. Keep the products where you are still the leader.

Our estimate: it is late 1985. You are still making memory chips and still losing money on them. The first samples of your new 386 processor are out. But the chip boom is over, and you have far too many people and plants for the business you have.

Our estimate: it is late 1985. You left memory a year early, so your losses are smaller. The first samples of your new 386 processor are out. But the chip boom is over, and you still have too many people and plants for the business you have.

It is late 1985. The first samples of your new 386 processor came out in October. But the chip boom ended in late 1984. Your costs were built for a company with $2 to 3 billion in yearly sales, and you are becoming a $1 to 1.5 billion company. Sales have dropped sharply, and profits have all but disappeared.
You have too many plants and too many people for the sales you have. Some of your plants are old and small. The 386 needs money for research and new machines.
How do you cut costs?
Cut deep once, not a little every month. But do not cut the future.
Our estimate: nobody loses a job this year, and people are grateful. But the old plants keep eating money, and the cuts are not deep enough. A year later you have to cut again.

Small, kind cuts feel fair, but they often only delay the hard choice and make the pain last longer. What would have worked: Close the old plants in one go, protect research, and tell people the plan honestly.
Our estimate: the numbers look better this year, but the 386 slips. New chips arrive late, and rivals get time to catch up.

In a tech company, research is the future. Cutting it to save today's jobs puts every job at risk later. What would have worked: Cut old plants and overhead, but keep paying for the products that will bring you back.

Over 1985 and 1986 Intel closed eight older, smaller plants and cut its workforce by 7,200 people, through layoffs and people leaving. It was the hardest time in its history. But it kept buying new equipment, and in 1986 it raised research spending to $228 million, 18% of its sales. Its factories became twice as productive in two years.
You made the painful cuts in the old parts of the company and protected the parts that would bring you back.

Our estimate: after your research cuts, the 386 is running late. For years, big buyers have demanded that a second company also make your chips, in case you fail to deliver. AMD did this for your earlier chips. Now you must decide who makes the 386.

Your 386 took four years and $100 million to build. For years, big buyers have demanded that a second company also make your chips, in case you fail to deliver. AMD did this for your earlier chips. But AMD has not given you the products you wanted in return, and your lawyers are in court to protect the code inside your chips.
Who gets to make your 386?
Sharing made sense when buyers had no other way to trust you. Do they still need it?
Our estimate: the 386 spreads fast, but so does the price war. Many makers sell your design, prices crash, and you earn little from the chip you spent $100 million to build.

You gave away your best product to rivals. The money from a winning chip went to everyone except you. What would have worked: Keep the 386 to yourself and win buyers' trust by building enough of it in more than one factory.
Our estimate: buyers feel safe, and the 386 sells well. But AMD sells the same chip at a lower price, and you share profits you could have kept.

It was the safe old habit. But the market had changed, and you no longer needed to share your best chip. What would have worked: Be the only maker, and show buyers you can deliver by building the 386 in two of your own factories.

After a fierce debate among Intel's top managers, Intel decided not to give the 386 to AMD or anyone else. To reassure buyers, it made the chip in two of its own factories. For 4.7 years Intel was the only company selling the 386. AMD's own version came only in March 1991, after legal fights.
You broke an old industry habit because the facts had changed. You kept your best product and found another way to earn buyers' trust.

IBM, which put your chip in its PC, is not interested in the 386. It is building its own version of your older 286 chip and wants more control over the PC. Meanwhile Compaq, a young company that makes IBM-compatible PCs, is ready to move fast.
How do you launch the 386?
Your most famous customer is not always your best partner for the next thing.
Our estimate: the 386 sits on the shelf for a year. Other chip makers get time to catch up, and your newest product earns almost nothing while you wait.
You let one customer set your timing. A great product is worth little if it waits for permission. What would have worked: Find a partner who wants to move now and launch with them.

Intel, Microsoft and Compaq worked closely together. On 9 September 1986 Compaq announced the Deskpro 386, the first PC with the 386 chip. IBM's first 386 PC came only in July 1987, nearly a year later. For the first time, a company other than IBM had moved the PC forward. By late 1987 Intel could not make 386 chips fast enough.
You did not wait for the giant. You found a hungry partner and let the market decide.
Our estimate: PC makers slowly test the 386, but nobody rushes to be first without IBM. The chip sells, but it takes longer to catch on.
Being open to everyone was fine, but a new product needs a champion who goes first. What would have worked: Work closely with one bold partner to launch fast, then sell to everyone.

In 1986 Intel lost $173 million. But the 386 sold faster than Intel could make it, and by late 1987 Intel expected a record profit. By 1992 it had 83% of the microprocessor market and made more than $1 billion a year. The memory company had become the processor company.
Our estimate: you let go of memory and bet on processors at the right time. The 386 sells faster than you can make it, and Intel becomes the company whose chips are inside most of the world's PCs.
Our estimate: Intel survives the memory crash and still makes good processors. But you shared too much or moved too slowly, and others take a big part of the PC chip market you could have owned.
Our estimate: you held on to memory chips and old habits for too long. The losses ate the money the processors needed, and Intel ends up as one more chip maker beaten by cheaper rivals.
Our estimate: three costly calls in a row. The board has lost its trust in you and asks someone else to lead Intel through the crash.
It's 1975 and you run Kodak, the biggest name in photography. You sell the film, the chemicals and the paper. Every holiday snap in America makes you money.

In December 1975, a 25-year-old Kodak engineer named Steve Sasson finishes a strange machine: an 8-pound box that takes a 100 by 100 pixel, black-and-white picture in 23 seconds and saves it to a cassette tape. You need a TV to see it. There is no film anywhere.
It's slow, ugly and blurry. But if it ever gets good, nobody will need your film.
What do you do with the digital camera?
The film division is nervous. Whatever you pick, they'll be watching.

Kodak patents the camera, but the executives who see it are not convinced. Sasson later recalled them doubting that anyone would want to look at their pictures on a television. No digital camera goes on sale.

Protecting your best business feels safe. But a new technology that looks worse at first can still replace you, and every year you wait, someone else learns it first. What would have worked: Give digital to a small, separate team that's allowed to compete with film, and fund it from film profits.
You give Sasson twenty engineers, a separate building and one rule: don't ask the film division for permission. Film keeps paying the bills while the team learns sensors, storage and screens.
You kept the cash machine running while buying time to learn the next one. A separate team can't be strangled by the business it's meant to replace.
You rush a camera into stores. It's bulky, slow and needs a television to view anything. Almost nobody buys it, and the loss shows up in your next annual report.

Right idea, wrong year. In 1975 there were no home computers and no screens worth viewing photos on. Being first is useless if customers can't use what you sell. What would have worked: Keep developing it in a separate team, and launch when screens and storage are ready.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. It is not digital yet, but it needs no film, and it is on the front pages with Sony's name on it. You can still fix this.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Retailers panic. Your digital team isn't surprised; they've been building something similar for six years.
August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Your early camera flopped, but the world just caught up with the idea.
The board is uneasy about your last call. A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
How do you respond to Sony?
Careful. One more bad call and the board starts asking questions about you.
Film still makes most of our money. But this time the world is watching.
The stock holds steady and the camera counters keep selling film. Inside Kodak, the message is clear: digital is not a career move. Your best engineers start taking calls from Japan.

Early versions of a disruptive product are always worse. Comparing today's quality hides the real question: how fast is it improving? What would have worked: Accept that digital is coming and start shifting money and people toward it while film is still strong.
Your market-intelligence chief, Vince Barabba, reports back: digital could replace film, but Kodak has roughly ten years to prepare. Kodak does little to prepare.

The study was right about the threat. The mistake was treating 'ten years' as permission to wait. A deadline is only useful if you start moving before it. What would have worked: Use the ten-year window to move money and talent into digital now, not in year nine.
You pull the 1975 prototype out of the cupboard and put its inventor in charge. It's six years late, but Kodak still has the money, the patents and the brand to catch up.
You announce that a growing share of film profits will fund digital imaging every year. Wall Street grumbles about lower margins. Your engineers stop job hunting.
You used the cash from the old business to pay for the new one while you still could. That's the move most incumbents make too late.
It's 2001. Your digital cameras are among the best sellers in America, and people are starting to put their photos online. Kodak has just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Digital cameras are finally taking off and Kodak is selling them, but film is still where the money is. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Kodak's new EasyShare digital cameras have made it number two in the US, but film still earns most of the money. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
Millions of people will soon put their photos online. But Kodak still earns its money from prints, paper and chemicals.
What is Ofoto for?
This is your last warning from the board. Get this one wrong and they'll find a new CEO.
Every photo that stays on a screen is a print we never sell. But maybe that's the point.
Renamed Kodak Gallery, the site grows to over 60 million users. But free accounts must keep buying prints or risk losing their photos.

You built the website around your old revenue instead of what customers wanted to do. The customer's job had changed from printing memories to sharing them. What would have worked: Make it a free place to share photos with friends, and earn from the audience instead of paper.

Uploads are free, albums are easy to share, and friends comment on each other's photos. Within a few years, Kodak owns the place where families keep their pictures, just as phones start getting cameras.
You followed the customer's new habit, sharing, even though it hurt print sales. Owning the audience is worth more than owning the paper.
Kodak cameras fly off the shelves and the brand looks modern again. But every competitor is selling cameras too, and prices fall every year.

Cameras were a real business, but a crowded one with thin margins. You gave up the part of digital that customers come back to every day. What would have worked: Keep the website and make it about sharing. That's where people would spend their time.
It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing across the industry, but your digital businesses are growing fast enough to carry the company. You have a strong hand. Don't waste it.
It's 2007. Film sales are collapsing. Your digital business is real but not yet big enough to replace what film used to earn. This is your last big decision.
It's 2007. Film sales are falling fast. This is your last chance to save the company.
You have patents, chemistry expertise, factories and a famous name. Film won't come back.
Where do you bet the company's future?
Whatever we pick, we can only afford to do it properly once.
You win shelf space, then lose money on every price cut. Within a few years, the phone in everyone's pocket takes good enough pictures, and the standalone camera market starts to shrink.

You chose a market where prices only go down and a bigger threat, the phone, was already arriving. What would have worked: Use what Kodak is best at, chemistry and materials, to enter new growing markets.

In February 2007 Kodak unveiled EasyShare all-in-one printers, claiming its ink could cut the cost of printing a photo by up to half. They went on sale in March. The printers never became the big new business Kodak needed.

Cheaper ink was a smart pitch for a shrinking habit. You bet on people printing photos at home just as they started keeping them on screens. What would have worked: Use Kodak's chemistry and materials know-how to enter new growing markets, as Fujifilm did.

You cut costs hard in film, then point your chemists at medical imaging, specialty films and materials. It's painful and slow, but new businesses start replacing what film used to earn. Fujifilm made a similar move and is still thriving.
You asked what Kodak was really good at, chemistry and materials, instead of what it used to sell. Skills travel to new markets; products don't.
By 2012, Kodak is a digital imaging and materials company. Film is a small, profitable corner of the business. Business schools teach your story as the incumbent that disrupted itself.
Kodak shrinks a lot, but it never goes bankrupt. You fixed enough, late enough, to keep the lights on. With a few earlier calls, it could have led the digital age.

On January 19, 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy. That April, Facebook buys Instagram, a photo-sharing app with 13 employees, for one billion dollars. The company that invented the digital camera lost the digital age.
Three bad calls. The board loses faith and replaces you. Your successor inherits a company that's falling behind, and the clock is still ticking.

It is 1998. For about 50 years, children have built with your plastic bricks. You run LEGOLAND parks in Denmark and England, and in 1996 you started a team to make computer games. But kids now love game consoles, and this year, for the first time in its history, LEGO loses money.

Since 1993 your sales have hardly grown. You keep adding new toys, but you are not selling more of them. Now you can make Star Wars sets. Some of your team also want more parks, more games, clothes and many new products.
How do you grow LEGO?
Kids still love to build. The question is how far from the brick you can go.

In 1999 LEGO launched its first Star Wars sets. They sold so well that LEGO made a profit again that year. LEGOLAND California opened too. LEGO also moved into electronics, video games, jewellery and learning centres, and it had three times as many products as before. But in 2000 LEGO lost 831 million kroner. It cut 1,500 jobs and stopped making clothes, watches and books.

Star Wars was a smart bet, because it still sold bricks. But parks, clothes and watches pulled money and attention away from the brick, and too many products made everything cost more. What would have worked: Take the Star Wars deal, because it sells bricks, but say no to side businesses that are not built from the brick.
Our estimate: Star Wars sets bring new fans to the brick. With fewer side businesses, your money and your best people stay on the toy kids love most, and costs stay under control.
You used a popular story to sell more of what you do best, and you did not spread yourself thin.
Our estimate: you keep things simple, but you miss the Star Wars boom. Kids who love films and games walk past your sets, and sales keep slipping.

Kids' lives were changing. Ignoring that change does not protect the brick; it makes the brick look old. What would have worked: Use popular stories like Star Wars to bring kids to the brick, while staying careful about side businesses.

Our estimate: it is 2002. Without film sets, your sales are flat. Your own new line, Bionicle, sells well: heroes you build from LEGO parts, with their own story. Your team wants to move further from the brick.

It is 2002. Your Star Wars and Harry Potter sets sell very well, but only in years when a new film comes out. Your own new line, Bionicle, is a hit: heroes you build from LEGO parts, with their own story. Your team wants to move further from the brick.
Which new toys do you bet on?
Every new toy should answer one question: does it make kids want to build?

In 2002 LEGO replaced DUPLO, its big bricks for small children, with a new brand called Explore in the United States. Parents did not see Explore as LEGO, and it did not sell. It cost about 500 million kroner. LEGO also launched Galidor, action figures with special parts and a TV show that LEGO paid for. The show was not popular, and the toys sold badly.

You swapped a brand parents trusted for one they did not know, and you made toys that were hardly LEGO at all. Both moved you away from the brick. What would have worked: Grow from the brick, like Bionicle did: new stories and new shapes, but always built from parts that fit with other LEGO parts.
Our estimate: shops sell more boxes, but each one makes less money. The real problem, too many costly products, stays hidden.

Lower prices bought some sales, but they did not fix what was wrong with the product range. What would have worked: Fix the range first: fewer, better sets built from the brick, and stories like Bionicle that sell every year.
Our estimate: lines like Bionicle give kids a reason to buy every year, not just in film years. DUPLO keeps its place with small children, and parents keep trusting the name.
You found something that worked and did more of it, without leaving the brick behind.

It is 2004. In 2003 LEGO lost about 1.4 billion kroner before tax, the biggest loss in its history. The company is almost out of cash and owes nearly $1 billion. Some sets have parts that cost more to make than the whole box sells for, and nobody knows which products make money. The owner family puts 800 million kroner of its own money in, and a new CEO takes over. That CEO is you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. Explore and Galidor have flopped, and money is running out. The board brings in a new CEO to save the company. That CEO is you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. Sales have been weak for years, and money is tight. The board wants a new plan, and it wants it from you.
Our estimate: it is 2004. LEGO is in better shape than many toy makers, but costs are high. The board wants a plan for the next ten years.
LEGO owns four LEGOLAND parks, a video game company and a huge range of products. You need cash fast, and you need to stop the losses.
Our estimate: LEGO owns LEGOLAND parks, a video game team and many products it does not need. Costs are too high for the money coming in.
Where do you start?
Ask one thing about every business: does it help kids build with LEGO bricks?
Our estimate: the bank lends you money, but the interest piles up. The parks and the games team keep eating cash, and the film you were waiting for does not come in time.
Borrowing to keep a broken business going only makes the hole deeper. What would have worked: Sell what others can run better, close what loses money, and spend your cash on the brick.

In 2004 LEGO cut about 1,000 jobs and closed its video game company. Some of its staff set up a new firm that published LEGO games made by an outside studio. Their LEGO Star Wars game came out in 2005 and sold 3.3 million copies by March 2006. DUPLO came back in 2004. In 2005 LEGO sold its four LEGOLAND parks to Merlin Entertainments, owned by Blackstone, for €375 million, and took a 30% stake in Merlin.
Our estimate: you sell the parks to a theme park company and keep a share. You close your game team and let a partner make LEGO games. The cash gives you room to fix the brick business.
You let go of businesses that did not need LEGO to own them, raised cash, and put all your effort back into the brick.
Our estimate: costs fall for a while, but the parks still need big money and the games still lose it. LEGO is smaller, but not more focused.

Cutting a little from everything feels fair, but it keeps the parts that drain you. What would have worked: Sell what others can run better, like theme parks, and let studios make LEGO games. Spend your cash on the brick.
LEGO makes about 13,000 different pieces. Every new piece costs money to design, make, store and ship, and many are used in only a few sets.
What do you do with all these pieces?
A good LEGO piece is one you can use in a hundred models, not one.

LEGO cut the number of different pieces it made from about 13,000 to about 6,000–6,500 over several years, and stopped making toys that did not sell. It put profit first and growth second. In 2005 LEGO made a profit of 505 million kroner, after losing 1.93 billion kroner in 2004. Sales grew 12% to 7.05 billion kroner, led by Bionicle, DUPLO, LEGO City and LEGO Star Wars.
Our estimate: with about half as many pieces, sets cost less to make and are easier to keep in stock. Designers get more creative inside clear limits, and profit starts to come back.
Fewer pieces meant lower costs everywhere, from the factory to the warehouse, and the old pieces could still build almost anything.
Our estimate: designers stay happy, but costs stay high. Warehouses fill with pieces few sets need, and many boxes still lose money.

Freedom without limits made LEGO expensive to run. Every extra piece had a cost that nobody was counting. What would have worked: Cut the list of pieces and make each new one prove it will be used in many sets.
Our estimate: shops get a cleaner range, but the factory still has to handle thousands of pieces. Costs fall a little, not a lot.
It fixed what customers see, but not the costs hidden in the factory. What would have worked: Cut the pieces too, not just the sets. That is where most of the cost hides.
LEGO is closing a factory in Switzerland and wants to make more bricks in countries where costs are lower. A big contract manufacturer called Flextronics offers to make many of your bricks for you.
How do you make bricks for less?
Your bricks must fit together perfectly, every time. Whoever makes them must care about that as much as you do.
Our estimate: quality stays perfect, but your costs stay far above other toy makers'. Each box earns less, and there is little money left for new ideas.

Pride in how you make things is good. But refusing to change where and how you make them leaves you too expensive. What would have worked: Move making to cheaper places, but in factories you own and run yourself.

From 2006 LEGO moved a large part of its making, especially DUPLO, to Flextronics plants in Hungary, the Czech Republic and Mexico. There were problems from the start. Parts ran short and LEGO could not make enough to meet demand; Flextronics could not even make enough DUPLO flowers. In 2008 LEGO ended the deal and took the work back. In 2009 it opened its own factories in Hungary and Mexico.

Cutting costs was right. But making perfect bricks was a core skill, and LEGO learned it could not hand that to someone else. What would have worked: Move making to cheaper places, but in your own factories, run by your own people.
Our estimate: it takes longer and costs more at first, but you keep control of quality, and shops never run short of your sets.
You cut costs without giving away the skill that makes LEGO special.

LEGO kept growing. In the first half of 2014 its sales were more than three times what they were in the first half of 2008. The LEGO Movie came out in 2014 and earned about $470 million around the world, and that year LEGO passed Mattel, the maker of Barbie, in half-year sales. By 2015 LEGO made more profit than any other toy company. A company that almost ran out of cash in 2003 was now one of the strongest in its industry.
Our estimate: you kept LEGO close to the brick and fixed problems early. LEGO grows year after year and becomes one of the most loved toy companies in the world.
Our estimate: LEGO survives and makes money again, but it is smaller and slower than it could have been. Other toy makers take the lead.
Our estimate: the losses never stop. The owner family has to sell LEGO to a bigger toy company, and the brick becomes just one brand among many.
Our estimate: three costly calls. The owner family loses trust in you and asks someone else to save LEGO.
You run Nestlé India. Maggi is the country's favourite instant noodles, a two-minute meal in millions of kitchens and hostel rooms. It makes up about 30% of your company's sales.

Food safety officers in Barabanki, Uttar Pradesh, picked up a Maggi batch for a routine check. A state lab now reports lead above the legal limit, and MSG, though your pack says no added MSG. Your company disputes the result: you add no MSG, and glutamate occurs naturally in some ingredients.
How do you respond to the report?
This is one batch in one district. But how you treat one batch tells people how you'll treat the next.
Nestlé appealed and asked for the samples to go to the central referral lab in Kolkata. That lab confirmed the findings. The problem did not go away. It grew.

Using the proper appeal was your right. But treating it only as a legal step left the public question, about the label and the lead, unanswered. What would have worked: Appeal if you disagree, but also fix the label and order fresh independent tests, then tell the public what you found.
Our estimate: the batch disappears, but the lab report doesn't. When it comes out later, saying nothing looks like hiding.
Silence feels safe until the news comes out. Then it looks like you had something to hide. What would have worked: Act in the open: test independently, fix the label, and tell people what you found.
Our estimate: it costs money and some awkward headlines, but when other states start testing, you already have your own independent results to show.
Being open early builds a store of trust you can draw on when things get worse.

April 2015. Uttar Pradesh orders a recall of a batch made in February 2014. Nestlé says that batch had already passed its best-before date. Other states start testing. Delhi reports that 10 of 13 samples are above its limit and bans sales for 15 days. On 3 June, Nestlé India's shares fall about 10%, their biggest one-day drop in nine years.
Your own independent tests are already public, but the bans are spreading state by state. Parents are worried.
The bans are spreading state by state, and some big shops have already taken Maggi off their shelves. Parents are worried.
What do you say and do?
You may be right about the science. The question is what worried parents need from you this week.

Nestlé said more than 1,000 batches had been tested and lead was within limits, and that only Uttar Pradesh had ordered a recall. More states banned sales, and big shops and the Indian army dropped Maggi. Many critics called the response slow.

You answered fear with numbers. Even if the numbers were right, parents heard a company protecting its sales. What would have worked: Take the product off the shelves yourself, say safety comes first, and let the tests speak later.
Our estimate: sales stop overnight and the cost is huge. But because you acted first, people see a company that puts their families first.
Putting safety ahead of sales, before anyone forced you, protects the one thing a food brand can't buy back: trust.
Our estimate: you follow each ban as it comes, but every new state makes headlines, and it looks like you only act when forced.
Following the rules state by state is reasonable, but it lets the crisis set the pace instead of you. What would have worked: Make one clear move yourself across the whole country.
Our estimate: the empty shelves make the news, but so does your choice. Then the national food regulator orders a recall of all approved Maggi variants and calls them unsafe.

On 5 June 2015, Nestlé announced it was withdrawing Maggi from shelves across India. The same day, the national food regulator ordered a recall of all nine approved variants and called them unsafe. About 38,000 tonnes of noodles were destroyed, burned in cement plants. Nestlé India reported a loss of Rs 64.4 crore for the quarter.
The regulator's order covers all nine variants, including ones that were never tested. You believe the testing process was unfair.
What do you do about the ban?
You can be right in court and still lose in people's kitchens. Think about both.

Nestlé challenged the order in the Bombay High Court. In August 2015 the court set the ban aside. It found that Nestlé had not been given a fair hearing, that the labs used were not accredited, and that the ban covered variants never tested. It ordered new tests in three accredited labs. The regulator later appealed to the Supreme Court.
You challenged the process, not the people, and asked for fair tests. That gave you a clear, public way back.
Our estimate: the ads make the fight personal. Officials dig in, and many people now see a big company bullying its regulator.
Attacking the people who keep food safe looks like you don't care about safety. What would have worked: Use the courts to ask for a fair process, and keep your public message about safety.
Our estimate: you avoid a public fight, but with no clear process for retesting, the noodles stay off the shelves for much longer.
Calm was good, but without a fair process to ask for, you had no clear way back. What would have worked: Respectfully ask a court for a fair process and accredited retests.
October 2015. All 90 samples in the court-ordered tests have come back clear, and three factories have started making Maggi again.
Our estimate: after a long wait, the noodles are cleared to return. You have one chance to win families back.
How do you bring Maggi back?
Coming back is not just restocking shelves. It is asking families to trust you again.
Our estimate: a new name confuses loyal fans and looks like you are hiding from Maggi's past.

Your brand's history is also its strength. Running from it throws away years of love. What would have worked: Bring Maggi back under its own name, carefully, once new batches have also passed the tests.
Our estimate: sales jump back quickly, but one bad test on a rushed batch could start the whole crisis again.
Speed brings sales back, but trust needs proof before volume. What would have worked: Wait until new batches also pass the tests, then return with a big, careful launch.
Nestlé waited until new batches also cleared the tests. On 9 November 2015, around Diwali, Maggi went back on sale in 100 cities, with an online shopping partner.
You came back with proof first and then a big, warm moment, giving families a reason to try Maggi again.
Our estimate: because you put families first from the start, Maggi comes back with its fans' trust intact and soon wins back almost all of the market.

Maggi came back. By October 2016, press reports put its share of instant noodles at 57%, against 75% before the crisis, with new rivals now on the shelf. In 2024 the national consumer commission dismissed the government's case, after tests at CFTRI, the lab the Supreme Court chose, found lead within limits.
Our estimate: the noodles come back, but families have moved on to rival brands, and Maggi never wins back its old place.
Our estimate: after three costly calls in a row, the board loses its trust in you and asks someone else to lead the company through the crisis.

It is 1981. An earlier Maruti company tried to build a small Indian car in Gurgaon, but it made only a handful of cars and was closed. Now the government has started a new company, Maruti Udyog, also in Gurgaon. You run it. Your team has no car experience. India's whole car market is only about 35,000 to 40,000 cars a year, mostly the big Ambassador and Padmini. Your target is 1,00,000 cars a year.

You need a foreign carmaker to share its know-how. Fiat, Peugeot, Volkswagen, Renault and Nissan have said no. Most others want to send their own staff and machines and run the show. Daihatsu from Japan was your best hope, but a message in February suggests it is not serious. Then another Japanese maker, Suzuki, sends a telex: it wants in.
Who do you build India's car with?
A famous name looks good on paper. But who really wants this deal, and who will teach us?
Our estimate: months go by in letters and meetings. In the end you get a deal, but late, and with a partner that sees India as a small side project.

Waiting for a big name cost time, and a partner that does not care much will not give you its best people. What would have worked: Pick the partner that is hungry for the deal and will commit its top people, even if it is smaller.

Talks with Suzuki began in April 1982. Suzuki's president met the Indian team himself, and its money offer was the best. On 2 October 1982 the two sides signed. Suzuki paid about USD 20.8 million for 26% of Maruti, and agreed to go up to 40% in five years.
You chose the partner that wanted you most. A smaller company that puts its top boss on your deal will teach you more than a giant that does not care.
Our estimate: the factory starts fast, but Indians only watch. Your people learn little, and every big decision is made far away.

The point was to build Indian skills. A partner who runs everything leaves you with a factory but no know-how. What would have worked: Pick a partner that will teach your own people and help Indian suppliers grow.

Suzuki has offered to help build an 800 cc car. Your research shows that more than 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities, on crowded roads. Today's cars, the Ambassador and Padmini, are big and old.

Our estimate: your new partner offers you a few of its models. Your research shows that more than 9 in 10 car trips in India carry four people or fewer, mostly inside cities. Today's cars, the Ambassador and Padmini, are big and old.
What do you build first?
Don't build the car you would like to drive. Build the one a clerk or a shopkeeper can buy.
